query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Engineering the surface of a powder‐metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA) to deliberately promote rapid in‐situ formation of a protective spinel/oxide film will yield superior tribo‐corrosion degradation resistance compared to conventional structural alloys under high-temperature, oxidizing, wear conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder-metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA with a homogeneous microstructure and finely distributed phases prior to any surface modification.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface/interface engineering treatment—using optimized spark plasma sintering parameters combined with controlled atmospheric exposure—to tailor the kinetics and morphology of the in-situ forming spinel/oxide film.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments with simultaneous mechanical (reciprocating wear) and oxidative (corrosive) attack, such as test setups in air at elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A deliberately engineered, adherent spinel/oxide surface film that forms rapidly under operational conditions and acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Under elevated temperature tribo-corrosive conditions, the engineered surface treatment triggers the rapid formation of a stable spinel/oxide film that prevents direct exposure of the underlying HEA to the corrosion environment and reduces wear by acting as a protective barrier.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated HEA is expected to show lower mass loss and reduced friction coefficient during high-temperature reciprocating wear tests compared to both conventional alloys and untreated HEA, indicating improved tribo-corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (mass loss, coefficient of friction, and microstructural integrity) observed for conventional structural alloys under similar high-temperature tribo-corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The protection is presumed effective in oxidizing environments where oxide/spinel formation is promoted; its efficacy under reducing conditions or in extremely aggressive corrosion media remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide film formation under dynamic tribological stresses and the long-term stability of the protective film under cyclical environmental variations require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA samples: one group subjected to the engineered surface treatment (aimed at promoting rapid spinel/oxide formation) and one untreated group. In addition, include a set of conventional structural alloy samples. Expose all samples to high-temperature reciprocating wear tests in an oxidizing environment. Analyze the evolution and stability of the surface film and record performance metrics during testing.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Characterization of the surface oxide/spinel film (using XRD, SEM, and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered HEA does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in mass loss reduction, lower friction coefficient, and evidence of a stable, adherent protective oxide/spinel film compared to both the untreated HEA and conventional alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Early work on HEAs for extreme environments has mainly concentrated on tailoring compositions and optimizing processing routes (e.g., powder metallurgy, spark plasma sintering) to enhance high‐temperature strength and oxidation resistance. For instance, PMC7515071 investigated an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA and found that, under reciprocating wear at elevated temperatures, the alloy developed an in‐situ spinel phase that reduced wear. Other studies focused on refractory HEAs and lightweight systems to improve overall corrosion or oxidation performance, but they did not fully address the combined tribological and corrosive challenges. Thus, the trend has been to build high-temperature structural performance and observe the beneficial (yet incidental) formation of protective surface films during wear.
decision.unsolved: While oxidation and corrosion resistance have been improved separately and some HEAs show promising wear reduction through in‐situ film formation, a deliberately engineered solution to simultaneously counter abrasive wear and corrosive attack (tribo-corrosion) under high-temperature conditions remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Deliberate promotion and control of a self-adaptive, adherent protective spinel/oxide surface film (for example, by tuning the in-situ formation kinetics and morphology of the passivating layer)
decision.why: Since PMC7515071 demonstrated that the formation of a spinel phase at higher temperatures can significantly improve wear resistance, the most plausible next step is to leverage surface or interface engineering to intentionally design the HEA’s surface so that it rapidly develops and maintains a stable, protective oxide/spinel film under tribo-corrosive conditions. This approach directly addresses the challenge of combined high-temperature wear and corrosion while preserving the underlying structural integrity.
